stories.title: A handover that fit on one page
stories.body: A week before leave I wrote a one-page handover: what is running, who to ask, and where things live. It took an evening. When I came back, nobody had needed to call me, and I felt calm about leaving.

stories.title: Telling my manager early
stories.body: I was nervous about the conversation, so I wrote down three things I wanted to agree on: dates, cover, and how often we would stay in touch. Having the list made it feel like planning, not asking permission.

stories.title: Five minutes was enough
stories.body: Some weeks all I managed was one line in my journal on my phone while feeding. I thought it did not count. Months later those lines turned into most of my resume summary.

stories.title: Explaining the gap without apologising
stories.body: I used to start every interview by apologising for my break. A friend suggested I lead with what I had done instead: a course, some volunteering, and running a household budget. The tone of the conversations changed.

stories.title: Practising with a peer
stories.body: I did two practice interviews with someone returning to a similar role. We swapped feedback kindly. By the real interview I had already said my answers out loud, and that made all the difference.

posts.body: I found it easier to write the handover as a list of questions people might ask me.

posts.name: Asha
posts.body: Today's tiny win: I wrote down one thing I fixed at work last year. Five minutes, done.

posts.name: Farah
posts.body: Voice notes while the baby naps have been a lifesaver for my journal.

posts.name: Nisha
posts.body: Tip: I list three things I did during my break at the start of every interview now.
